### SUMMARY

### Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures

Imposes 5% tax on certain taxpayers with assets over $1 billion; revenue primarily for health care. Exempts revenues from constitutional requirements for school funding and spending limit. **Fiscal Impact:** Temporary revenue increase of tens of billions of dollars spread over several years from wealth tax on billionaires. YES A YES vote on this measure means: The state would collect a one-time tax from billionaires equal to 5 percent of their wealth.

NO A NO vote on this measure means: The state would *not* collect a one-time tax from billionaires equal to 5 percent of their wealth.

PRO Vote YES on 40 to tax billionaires. ## IMPOSES ONE-TIME TAX ON CERTAIN TAXPAYERS. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT AND STATUTE.

## ANALYSIS BY THE LEGISLATIVE ANALYST

### BACKGROUND

***California Is Home to Many Billionaires.*** Several of the wealthiest people in the world live in California. Wealth is the value of all the things a person owns. Wealth is different from income, which is how much a person earns in a set period of time, like one year. A person’s wealth typically is measured by their net worth. A person’s net worth is the value of all the things they own, like stocks, businesses, or other investments, minus their debts. California is home to a few hundred people with net worth over $1 billion, often called billionaires. Many of these billionaires gained their wealth as executives or investors in California technology companies.

***Health Care Is a Major Category of State Spending.*** The state and federal government spend over $200 billion per year on state health care programs. Most state health care spending is for Medi-Cal, the state’s health insurance program for low-income people. State spending also supports public health programs, mental health care, and drug and alcohol treatment.

### PROPOSAL

***Establishes One-Time Wealth Tax on Billionaires.*** Under Proposition 40, billionaires who were residents of California on January 1, 2026 would have to pay a one-time state tax equal to 5 percent of their net worth. The tax would be due in 2027. Taxpayers would have the option to spread the payments over five years but would have to pay more to do so. Real estate, pensions, and retirement accounts generally would be excluded from the tax.

***Most of the Money Must Be Spent on Health Care.*** The state would decide how and when to spend the money from the wealth tax, but it would have to be spent on certain types of services. Ninety percent of the money would have to be spent on health care services for the public. The rest would have to be spent on education, food assistance, and administration of the wealth tax. Existing rules in the State Constitution that limit spending and require the state to spend a certain amount on schools and community colleges would not apply to this money.

### FISCAL EFFECTS

***Temporary State Revenue Increase From Wealth Tax.*** The state probably would collect tens of billions of dollars from the wealth tax. This temporary increase in state tax collections would be spread across several years. Exactly when and how much the state would collect is very hard to predict for many reasons. For example, it is hard to know what actions billionaires would take to reduce the amount of tax they pay. Also, much of the wealth is based on stock prices, which are always changing.

***Possible Ongoing Decrease in State Income Tax Revenues.*** California billionaires, like all those earning money in the state, currently pay state taxes on their annual income. Billionaires may respond to a new wealth tax in ways that reduce their income tax payments. For example, some billionaires may decide to leave California. The income taxes they currently pay to the state also would go away. These responses probably would reduce state revenues by less than $1 billion per year. This could mean less money for the state’s General Fund, which is the account that pays for most public services, including education, health care, and prisons.

***State Costs to Administer the Wealth Tax.*** The state would have costs to determine how much wealth tax is owed and to collect tax payments. These costs could be tens of millions of dollars per year for several years. These costs would be paid from the new wealth tax revenues.

 **California Proposition 40**, the **One-Time Wealth Tax for State-Funded Health Care Programs Initiative**, is on the [ballot](/California_2026_ballot_propositions "California 2026 ballot propositions") in [California](/California "California") as an [combined initiated constitutional amendment and state statute](/Combined_initiated_constitutional_amendment_and_state_statute "Combined initiated constitutional amendment and state statute") on [November 3, 2026](/California_2026_ballot_propositions "California 2026 ballot propositions").[\[1\]](#cite_note-text-1) 

A "**yes**" vote supports this initiative to levy a one-time 5% tax on the accumulated wealth of taxpayers and trusts with covered assets valued over $1 billion, including shares of capital stock, bonds or other evidences of indebtedness, and any legal or equitable interest, to fund state health care programs, food assistance programs, and public education.

A "**no**" vote opposes this initiative to levy a one-time 5% tax on the accumulated wealth of taxpayers and trusts with covered assets valued over $1 billion, including shares of capital stock, bonds or other evidences of indebtedness, and any legal or equitable interest, to fund state health care programs, food assistance programs, and public education.

  
 

[Competing ballot measures in 2026](/Superseding_initiative "Superseding initiative")

Two measures — [Proposition 41, the Prohibit Excluding New State Taxes from Spending Limit and Require Special Tax Audits Initiative](/California_Proposition_41,_Prohibit_Excluding_New_State_Taxes_from_Spending_Limit_and_Require_Special_Tax_Audits_Initiative_\(2026\) "California Proposition 41, Prohibit Excluding New State Taxes from Spending Limit and Require Special Tax Audits Initiative (2026)") and [Proposition 42, the Prohibit New Taxes on Retirement Holdings, Personal Assets, and Savings Initiative](/California_Proposition_42,_Prohibit_New_Taxes_on_Retirement_Holdings,_Personal_Assets,_and_Savings_and_Limit_Retroactive_Taxes_Initiative_\(2026\) "California Proposition 42, Prohibit New Taxes on Retirement Holdings, Personal Assets, and Savings and Limit Retroactive Taxes Initiative (2026)") — are also on the November 3 ballot in California and contain competing measure provisions that would nullify Proposition 40 if all the measures are approved but Propositions 41 and 42 receive more votes than Proposition 40. Proposition 40 also contains a competing measure provision that would nullify Propositions 41 and 42 if Proposition 40 receives more votes.

## Overview

### What would the initiative do?

*See also: [Measure design](#Measure_design) and [2026 competing California tax measures](#2026_competing_California_tax_measures)*

The initiative would enact a one-time tax of 5% on the accumulated wealth of taxpayers and trusts with covered assets valued over $1 billion, including shares of capital stock, bonds or other evidences of indebtedness, and any legal or equitable interest. The tax would be retroactive and apply to taxpayers residing in the state as of January 1, 2026. The tax would be due with an individual's 2027 tax filings. The initiative would allow individuals to pay the tax in five equal installments beginning in 2027, with each subsequent payment subject to an annual deferral charge of 7.5% of the remaining unpaid balance.[\[1\]](#cite_note-text-1) 

The initiative would create the 2026 Billionaire Tax Reserve Fund, where all taxes, interest, and penalties resulting from the initiative would be deposited. The fund would have two sub-accounts: the Billionaire Tax Health account, where 90% of the revenue would be deposited, and the Billionaire Tax Education and Food Assistance Account with the remaining 10% of revenue. The initiative would fund Medi-Cal and other health coverage programs for low- and moderate-income individuals; health care access, benefits, and services; public education from K-14; and food assistance programs such as CalFresh, CalFAP, CalFood, or California's Universal Meals Program for school meals.[\[1\]](#cite_note-text-1) 

Two measures — [Proposition 41, the Prohibit Excluding New State Taxes from Spending Limit and Require Special Tax Audits Initiative](/California_Proposition_41,_Prohibit_Excluding_New_State_Taxes_from_Spending_Limit_and_Require_Special_Tax_Audits_Initiative_\(2026\) "California Proposition 41, Prohibit Excluding New State Taxes from Spending Limit and Require Special Tax Audits Initiative (2026)") and [Proposition 42, the Prohibit New Taxes on Retirement Holdings, Personal Assets, and Savings Initiative](/California_Proposition_42,_Prohibit_New_Taxes_on_Retirement_Holdings,_Personal_Assets,_and_Savings_and_Limit_Retroactive_Taxes_Initiative_\(2026\) "California Proposition 42, Prohibit New Taxes on Retirement Holdings, Personal Assets, and Savings and Limit Retroactive Taxes Initiative (2026)") — are also on the November 3 ballot in California and contain competing measure provisions that would nullify Proposition 40 if all the measures are approved but Propositions 41 and 42 receive more votes than Proposition 40. Proposition 40 also contains a competing measure provision that would nullify Propositions 41 and 42 if Proposition 40 receives more votes. 

### How would net worth be calculated?

*See also: [Measure design](#Measure_design)*

To determine an individual's net worth, the initiative would account for the following assets:[\[1\]](#cite_note-text-1) 

*   publicly traded securities at their market value on December 31, 2026;
*   private business interests;
*   assets under a sole proprietorship;
*   grantor trusts;
*   art, collectibles, intellectual property, vehicles, other financial instruments not publicly traded, and debts or liabilities owed to the individual ($5 million exclusion of total combined asset value from net worth);
*   Roth IRA or other Roth-type retirement accounts valued above $10 million;
*   property valued at more than $1 million transferred after October 15, 2025, for less than fair market value; and
*   dependent's assets in excess of $50,000.

Real estate and pensions would be excluded from the calculation of net worth.[\[1\]](#cite_note-text-1) 

The initiative would account for the following debts as reductions to an individual's net worth:[\[1\]](#cite_note-text-1) 

*   recourse debts for which the individual is personally liable;
*   nonrecourse debts up to the value of the collateral securing them; and
*   debts and other liabilities resulting from a sole proprietorship but not from a partnership, limited liability company, or other business entity.

### Have other states enacted similar taxes?

*See also: [Wealth tax ballot measures](#Wealth_tax_ballot_measures) and [Ballot measures related to income and wealth taxes, 2026](/Ballot_measures_related_to_income_and_wealth_taxes,_2026 "Ballot measures related to income and wealth taxes, 2026")*

The California wealth tax initiative would be the first ballot measure in the country to enact such a tax. In 2023, Texas voters approved [Proposition 3](/Texas_Proposition_3,_Prohibit_Taxes_on_Wealth_or_Net_Worth_Amendment_\(2023\) "Texas Proposition 3, Prohibit Taxes on Wealth or Net Worth Amendment (2023)") by a margin of 68% to 32%, amending the state constitution to prohibit the state legislature from enacting a wealth tax or net worth tax in the future. 

Additionally, in 2026, there are nine statewide ballot measures in six states related to income and wealth tax policy. Of these measures, two would allow, create, or increase income taxes; five would prohibit, cap, or decrease income taxes; one would allow, create, or increase wealth taxes; and one would prohibit, cap, or decrease wealth taxes.

Wealth tax on taxpayers and trusts with covered assets valued over $1 billion

The initiative would levy a one-time tax of 5% on taxpayers and trusts with covered assets valued over $1 billion, including shares of capital stock, bonds or other evidences of indebtedness, and any legal or equitable interest. A married couple would be considered one individual. The tax would be retroactive and apply to any taxpayer residing in the state as of January 1, 2026. For individuals with net worth between $1 billion and $1.1 billion, the tax rate would be reduced by 0.1% (but not below 0%) for each $2 million their net worth falls below $1.1 billion. The tax would be due with an individual's 2027 tax filings.[\[1\]](#cite_note-text-1)

  
 

The initiative would allow individuals to pay the tax in five equal installments beginning in 2027, with each subsequent payment subject to an annual deferral charge of 7.5% of the remaining unpaid balance.[\[1\]](#cite_note-text-1)

Net worth calculation

To determine an individual's net worth, the initiative would account for the following assets:[\[1\]](#cite_note-text-1)

*   publicly traded securities at their market value on December 31, 2026;
*   private business interests;
*   assets under a sole proprietorship;
*   grantor trusts;
*   art, collectibles, intellectual property, vehicles, other financial instruments not publicly traded, and debts or liabilities owed to the individual ($5 million exclusion of total combined asset value from net worth);
*   Roth IRA or other Roth-type retirement accounts valued above $10 million;
*   property valued at more than $1 million transferred after October 15, 2025, for less than fair market value; and
*   dependent's assets in excess of $50,000.

Real estate and pensions would be excluded from the calculation of net worth.[\[7\]](#cite_note-lao-7) 

The initiative would account for the following debts as reductions to an individual's net worth:[\[1\]](#cite_note-text-1) 

*   recourse debts for which the individual is personally liable;
*   nonrecourse debts up to the value of the collateral securing them; and
*   debts and other liabilities resulting from a sole proprietorship but not from a partnership, limited liability company, or other business entity.

The following debts or liabilities would not lower an individual's net worth:[\[1\]](#cite_note-text-1) 

*   related-party debts;
*   charitable pledges made after October 15, 2025; and
*   contingent liabilities with outcomes uncertain within five years.

Revenue allocation

The initiative would create the 2026 Billionaire Tax Reserve Fund, where all taxes, interest, and penalties resulting from the initiative would be deposited. The fund would have two sub-accounts: the Billionaire Tax Health account, where 90% of the revenue would be deposited, and the Billionaire Tax Education and Food Assistance Account with the remaining 10% of revenue. The initiative would require the health account to fund Medi-Cal and other health coverage programs for low- and moderate-income individuals, as well as health care access, benefits, and services. The initiative would require revenue in the education account to fund public education from K-14, reductions in federal or state appropriations, and reductions in food assistance programs such as CalFresh, CalFAP, CalFood, or California's Universal Meals Program for school meals.[\[1\]](#cite_note-text-1)

  
 

The initiative contains a provision that would exclude the revenue generated by the tax from the state’s General Fund when calculating the state minimum guarantee for education funding, which was enacted by [Proposition 98](/California_Proposition_98,_Mandatory_Education_Spending_Initiative_\(1988\) "California Proposition 98, Mandatory Education Spending Initiative (1988)") in 1988.

### Constitutional changes

*See also: [Article XIII, California Constitution](/Article_XIII,_California_Constitution "Article XIII, California Constitution")*

The ballot measure would amend [Section 37 of Article XIII](/Article_XIII,_California_Constitution#Section_37 "Article XIII, California Constitution") of the [California Constitution](/California_Constitution "California Constitution"). The following underlined text would be added:[\[1\]](#cite_note-text-1) 

*Note*: Hover over the text and scroll to see the full text. 

Sec. 37. 

(a) This Section authorizes and enables a one-time tax on the accumulated wealth of California billionaires, imposed on those individuals who are California residents within the meaning of Sections 17014 and 17015.5 of the Revenue and Taxation Code as of the tax obligation date as defined in the 2026 Billionaire Tax Act. 

(b) The following definitions apply to this Section: 

(1) "Act" refers to the 2026 Billionaire Tax Act. 

(2) "Reserve Fund" refers to the 2026 Billionaire Tax Reserve Fund, created by this Act. 

(c) Notwithstanding any other provision of the Constitution, the Act provides for taxation on all forms of personal property and wealth, whether tangible or intangible, and allows for the classification of personal property and wealth for differential taxation or for exemption, for the purpose of imposing the one-time tax on the wealth of California billionaires. Personal property and wealth that is so taxed includes, but is not limited to, shares of capital stock, bonds or other evidences of indebtedness, and any legal or equitable interest therein. 

(d) The 2026 Billionaire Tax Reserve Fund is hereby created in the State Treasury. All revenues from the Act—including taxes, interest, and penalties, and less refunds—shall be deposited in the State Treasury by the State Controller to the credit of the Reserve Fund. After accounting for administrative expenses as provided by law, the Controller shall allocate and transfer the remaining moneys in the Reserve Fund to the following sub-accounts, which are hereby created: 90% to the Billionaire Tax Health Account and 10% to the Billionaire Tax Education and Food Assistance Account. The moneys in the Billionaire Tax Health Account and the Billionaire Tax Education and Food Assistance Account shall be allocated as provided by law. 

(e) Notwithstanding any other law, the Reserve Fund is a special fund, permanently separate and apart from the General Fund or any other state fund or account. The taxes and the moneys resulting from the Act shall not be considered to be part of the General Fund, as that term is used in Chapter 1 (commencing with Section 16300) of Part 2 of Division 4 of Title 2 of the Government Code; and shall not be considered "General Fund revenues," "state revenues," "moneys," or "proceeds of taxes" under Section 8 of Article XIIIB for the purposes of any section of Article XIIIB, or Sections 8 or 8.5 of Article XVI. Any revenue raised through the Act shall also not be considered "personal income taxes paid on net capital gains" for purposes of Section 20 of Article XVI. The taxes levied by this Act are not "ad valorem taxes on real property" for purposes of Section 1 of Article XIIIA. To the extent any provision of Article XIIIA would otherwise be construed to limit, restrict, or apply to the rate, base, valuation, or imposition of the tax authorized by this Section, that provision shall not apply to, and is superseded by, this Section. Notwithstanding Section 16305.7 of the Government Code, any interest or dividends earned on moneys in the Reserve Fund shall be retained in the Reserve Fund and used solely for the specific purposes set forth in this subdivision and as provided by the Act. 

(f) "Appropriations subject to limitation" of each entity of government and the state under Article XIIIB shall not include appropriations of revenue from the Reserve Fund. No adjustment in the appropriations limit of any entity of government shall be required pursuant to Section 3 of Article XIIIB as a result of revenue being deposited in or appropriated from the Reserve Fund. 

(g) Except as provided in Sections 16310 and 16381 of the Government Code as those sections read on January 1, 2025, and except as otherwise provided in this Act, moneys in the Reserve Fund shall not be borrowed, loaned, or otherwise transferred to the General Fund or any other state or local fund or account. Moneys deposited into the Reserve Fund shall only be used for the specific purposes provided by law. Action shall not be taken that permanently or temporarily changes the status of the Reserve Fund or borrows, diverts, or appropriates the moneys in the Reserve Fund in a manner inconsistent with this subdivision. 

(h) Notwithstanding Section 32 or any other provision of law, a facial challenge to the 2026 Billionaire Tax Act is authorized to be adjudicated through a validation action under Chapter 6 of Part 27 of the Revenue and Taxation Code, Section 50314 without requiring the payment of the tax claimed to be facially invalid. This subdivision is adopted without implication as to current authority or the development of law other than this Act. Nothing in this subdivision limits any taxpayer's right to pay a tax imposed under this Act and seek a refund or judicial review, or to bring any other action that is otherwise authorized by law and not inconsistent with this subdivision.[\[8\]](#cite_note-quotedisclaimer-8)

California voters are souring on a Nov. 3 ballot measure to impose a one-time tax on billionaires to help fund healthcare programs, a proposal that has triggered one of the most expensive political battles in state history.

Half of likely voters plan to vote against Proposition 40, [the proposed wealth tax](https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-40-billionaire-tax-voter-guide) on billionaires’ assets, while 42% support it, according to a new poll by UC Berkeley’s Institute of Governmental Studies that was co-sponsored by the Los Angeles Times. The findings mark a significant decline in support of the measure, which was crafted by an influential California healthcare union to compensate for an estimated $100 billion in federal healthcare cuts approved by President Trump and congressional Republicans.

The survey also found that a solid majority of likely voters opposed Proposition 39, which would require Californians to provide identification when voting and election officials to verify registered voters are U.S. citizens. The findings come as the Trump administration continues to attack California as a haven for voter fraud, including unfounded allegations of rampant illegal voting by undocumented immigrants.

### [Your guide to Proposition 40: California’s billionaire tax proposal](https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-40-billionaire-tax-voter-guide)

Prop 40, which would tax the assets of California billionaires to mostly fund healthcare, has divided Democratic politicians, labor unions and other groups.

 Oct. 1, 2026 

Mark DiCamillo, the poll’s director, said previous surveys showed support for Proposition 40 has been fragile, and the most recent shows its prospects have dimmed as election day approaches. 

 

The increase in opposition to Proposition 40 is “broad-based and spans virtually all major segments of the electorate,” DiCamillio said. The ballot measure was leading in a Berkeley poll conducted just six weeks ago, albeit by a slim margin, so its reversal of fortune is significant, he said. 

The declining support comes after an onslaught of money spent opposing Proposition 40, including a torrent of television and social media ads airing everywhere from NFL games to “Everybody Loves Raymond” reruns. Nearly $368 million has been contributed to efforts opposing the billionaire tax, while $36 million has been donated to support the proposed levy.

Proposition 40 would impose a one-time 5% tax on the assets of billionaires who resided in California as of Jan. 1, with some exceptions. Democrats and their allies are splintered over the proposal. Some, including Gov. Gavin Newsom, argue it will prompt the wealthy to flee California, further harming its volatile budget, which is dependent on the state’s richest residents. The California Democratic Party and leading progressives support the measure, with Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) calling it a modest tax necessary to help Californians struggling because of cuts imposed by Republicans to pay for tax breaks for the wealthy.

While Republican voters overwhelmingly oppose Proposition 40, nearly two-thirds of Democrats support it and more than a quarter opposing it. There is also a generational divide, with 6 out of 10 voters 65 years old or older opposing the measure, while more than two-thirds of those under 30 supporting it, according to the poll. 

The findings are similar to a Public Policy Institute of California poll released Tuesday, which found 52% of likely voters would vote against Proposition 40, while 46% supported it.

The campaign against the wealth tax, funded by some of California’s richest tech moguls, is centered on three intertwined ballot initiatives: Proposition 40 and Propositions 41 and 42, both of which would undercut Proposition 40 through a series of changes to state tax laws and spending restrictions. 

 

Proposition 41 would [cut wasteful government spending](https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-41-tax-audit-voter-guide) by requiring audits of new state special taxes and would bar new state taxes that are exempt from a state spending limit. Proposition 42 would prohibit new taxes on retirement holdings, individually owned assets and other personal savings. Both Propositions 41 and 42 would nullify the billionaire tax if it passes, provided either measure receives more votes.

A plurality of voters oppose Propositions 41 and 42, a reversal from just six week ago, according to the poll.

In mid-September, voters were closely divided about Proposition 41 [— 37% in favor and 33% opposed —](https://escholarship.org/uc/item/2zw023kt) with a large number of undecided. In the current poll, 38% of likely voters favor the measure and 47% oppose it. Proposition 42 led by 9 percentage points in the Berkeley/L.A. Times poll in September — 43% in favor and 34% opposed. Now, 43% of likely voters support it and 45% oppose it.

DiCamillo said backers of a ballot measure also should be concerned any time support registers below 50%, since voters who are undecided or unsure tend to vote no.

“It’s below 50%, and it’s trending down. Both of those are ominous signs,” DiCamillo said. Proposition 42 is “still very close. I’m not saying it’s definitely going down, but it’s moving in the wrong direction late in the campaign, and usually movement in a late poll is even more significant than the actual numbers themselves.”

He added that while many voters were unaware the two proposed ballot measures were designed as poison pills to kill the billionaire tax, among those who knew, the opposition was significantly greater.

If all three measures fail, that still would be a victory for the billionaires who spent aggressively to tank the wealth tax.

Another notable finding was voters’ support of Proposition 3, which would [make permanent a higher income tax rate on the wealthy](https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-3-high-income-tax-voter-guide) that funds education. A majority of voters — 54% — support continuing the levy, while 37% oppose it, according to the poll. DiCamillo says the disparity in support of the proposed billionaire tax and the extension of the existing wealth tax has been consistent in IGS’s polls, and is likely because of the differing foundations of the levies.

 

“Proposition 3 is already in place, and if you read the fiscal impact, if this were to pass, it maintains $5 billion to $15 billion of annual funding,” he said, “It’s a big revenue generator, and I think that is something that’s already in place.”

“Voters kind of understand the progressive nature of California’s tax system, and they kind of support that, but they don’t support nearly as much the idea of some new kind of tax, the wealth tax, which is taxing assets rather than income,” he said. “So that’s the distinction.”

These ballot measures are among [14 that voters will decide](https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-07-06/2026-california-propositions-voter-guide-billionaires-tax-voter-id-homebuyers-money-tax-hike-limits) on Nov. 3, as well as statewide, congressional, local and judicial elections.

The measure also would require the California secretary of state and county election officials to verify that registered voters are U.S. citizens by “using government data,” which according to supporters could include information in the federal Social Security Administration database, jury summons information and other government records.

 

Nearly 6 in 10 likely voters oppose the effort, while more than a third support it, split largely along party lines. More than half of voters who are registered as “no party preference” or with a smaller political party oppose the proposal, which DiCamillo said was an indication of trouble for the proposition given the state’s Democratic majority electorate and the proximity of the election.

“It’s hard for Republicans to push something over the finish line by themselves,” he said.

Other prominent ballot measures:

*   Proposition 43, which would [prohibit local governments](https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-43-threshold-local-special-tax-voter-guide) from imposing certain new special taxes unless two-thirds of voters approve the proposal. Such proposals need a simple majority vote to be approved. While 46% of likely voters oppose the proposal, 36% support it, challenging numbers this close to election day, DiCamillo said. “It needs to get to 50,” he said. “We’ll see how you do that this late in the campaign.”

*   Proposition 4, which would [repeal a prohibition of public financing of campaigns](https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-4-public-campaign-financing-voter-guide), allowing state and local governments to support candidates if they abide by several rules. Likely voters are evenly split about the proposal, with 41% supporting it and opposing it, and 18% undecided. “It’s close, but it’s still below 50%. Most voters tend to vote no in the late going if they’re not convinced,” DiCamillo said, adding that he viewed the lack of support among voters who do not affiliate with a political party as a signal of potential failure.

The poll of 2,787 registered California voters was conducted online in English and Spanish Oct. 19-25 and has a margin of error of about 3 percentage points in either direction.

## BECERRA PRESERVES WIDE LEAD OVER HILTON; ENTHUSIASM GAP FAVORS DEMOCRATS IN CONGRESSIONAL RACES; SOLID MAJORITY FAVOR HIGH-EARNER INCOME TAX MEASURE

SAN FRANCISCO, October 27, 2026—A week ahead of Election Day, Californians are exceptionally pessimistic about the direction of the country, the state, and the economy. Support for a high-profile initiative that would tax billionaires appears to be eroding. Democrat Xavier Becerra maintains a commanding lead over Republican Steve Hilton in the race for governor. And Democrats are far more excited than Republicans or independents about voting in congressional races. These are among the key findings from a statewide survey released today by the Public Policy Institute of California.

Eighty-two percent of adult Californians think things in the United States are generally going in the wrong direction, the highest share holding this pessimistic view since PPIC began asking about the national outlook two decades ago. Nearly eight in ten predict bad economic conditions in both the state and the nation over the next 12 months, a high not matched since the depths of the pandemic and Great Recession.

“If you’re looking for one word to describe Californians’ mood as they are filling out their ballots, it would be gloomy—very gloomy,” said Mark Baldassare, PPIC Statewide Survey director and Miller Chair in Public Policy. “Affordability continues to be a central concern, with majorities across demographic groups saying their incomes are not keeping up with inflation.”

In the race for governor, Democrat Xavier Becerra has a 24 point lead over Republican Steve Hilton (61% to 37%), including a 13 point lead among independent likely voters. Californians say they are largely satisfied with their choices for governor, although that satisfaction appears to vary significantly by age: while nearly 70 percent of likely voters 55 and older are pleased with their gubernatorial choices, only half of younger voters aged 18 to 34 are satisfied.

More key findings from the survey:

*   **Billionaire wealth tax falls below majority support:** Forty-six percent of likely voters say they will vote yes on Proposition 40, a controversial citizens’ initiative that would impose a one-time tax of up to 5 percent on taxpayers with assets over $1 billion. Last month, 52 percent of likely voters said they would support the measure.

    “Since last month, we’ve seen declining support for Prop 40, particularly among Democrats and independents,” said Baldassare. “Propositions 41 and 42, which could effectively nullify Prop 40 even if it was passed, are now polling better than the billionaire tax.”

    While support for the billionaire wealth tax appears to be eroding, a majority of likely voters back Proposition 3, which would make a temporary marginal income tax on high earners permanent. Among Democrats, 80 percent support Proposition 3, while 64 percent support the billionaire wealth tax.

*   **Enthusiasm gap favors Democrats in congressional races:** Seventy-one percent of Democratic likely voters say they are more enthusiastic than usual about voting in congressional elections, compared to 46 percent of Republicans. The partisan enthusiasm gap is larger than it was ahead of the 2024 general election.

    Unhappiness with the Trump administration is likely playing a role. Seventy-eight percent of California adults disapprove of the way Donald Trump is handling his job as president—the president’s highest disapproval rating among Californians during his two terms in office. Since the beginning of the year, the president’s approval ratings have dropped most acutely among independents, from 25 percent in February to 16 percent in October.

*   **Majorities back bond measures, oppose tax restrictions:** Majorities of California likely voters back the three borrowing measures on the November ballot. More than 60 percent support Propositions 1 and 37, which would authorize tens of billions in bonds for housing programs. Fifty-seven percent say they will vote yes on Proposition 38, which would authorize $8.4 billion in bonds for immunology research. A majority also support Proposition 2, which increases the amount of revenue the state can deposit into a rainy day fund.

    A majority of likely voters oppose Proposition 43, which would make it more difficult to increase local taxes. A slim majority oppose Proposition 45 (50% oppose, 46% approve), which would modify the state’s marquee environmental law to speed construction of some new developments.

*   **Californians are skeptical about the need for voter ID:** Nearly 60 percent of likely voters oppose Proposition 39, a citizens’ initiative that would require government-issued ID at the polls. Despite federal allegations of rampant voter fraud, 63 percent of likely voters have a great deal or quite a lot of confidence in the system in which votes are cast and counted in California.

**About the Survey**

The Californians and Their Government survey on state, local, and national issues is supported with funding from the Arjay R. and Frances F. Miller Foundation. The findings are based on responses from 1,728 California adult residents. The sampling error is ±3.0 percent at the 95 percent confidence level for the total unweighted sample and ±3.8 percent for the 1,086 likely voters. Interviewing took place from October 16–22, 2026. For more information, please see the methodology section in the full survey report.

Mark Baldassare is statewide survey director at PPIC, where he holds the Arjay and Frances Fearing Miller Chair in Public Policy. He is founder of the PPIC Statewide Survey, which he has directed since 1998.
